claim: Transcripts of neuronal mitochondrial genes are strongly suppressed in central nervous system inflammation.
source: While transcripts of neuronal mitochondrial genes are strongly suppressed in central nervous system inflammation, it is unknown whether this results in mitochondrial dysfunction and whether an increase of mitochondrial function can rescue neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the gene expression analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Predominantly genes of the electron transport chain are suppressed in inflamed mouse neurons.
source: Here, we show that predominantly genes of the electron transport chain are suppressed in inflamed mouse neurons, resulting in impaired mitochondrial complex IV activity.
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Suppression of electron transport chain genes results in impaired mitochondrial complex IV activity.
source: Here, we show that predominantly genes of the electron transport chain are suppressed in inflamed mouse neurons, resulting in impaired mitochondrial complex IV activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by COX histochemistry data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial complex IV activity is associated with post-translational inactivation of PGC-1α.
source: This was associated with post-translational inactivation of the transcriptional co-regulator proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased phosphorylation of PGC-1α at serine 570 in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a led to increased numbers of mitochondria in mice.
source: In mice, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a, which encodes for PGC-1α, led to increased numbers of mitochondria, complex IV activity, and maximum respiratory capacity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mtDNA quantification data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a led to increased complex IV activity.
source: In mice, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a, which encodes for PGC-1α, led to increased numbers of mitochondria, complex IV activity, and maximum respiratory capacity.
evidence: This is shown by COX histochemistry in Figure 3D.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a led to increased maximum respiratory capacity.
source: In mice, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a, which encodes for PGC-1α, led to increased numbers of mitochondria, complex IV activity, and maximum respiratory capacity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oxygen consumption rate measurements in Figure 3E.

claim: Ppargc1a-overexpressing neurons showed a higher mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Moreover, Ppargc1a-overexpressing neurons showed a higher mitochondrial membrane potential that related to an improved calcium buffering capacity.
evidence: This is shown by TMRE fluorescence measurements in Figure 3F.

claim: Higher mitochondrial membrane potential in Ppargc1a-overexpressing neurons relates to improved calcium buffering capacity.
source: Moreover, Ppargc1a-overexpressing neurons showed a higher mitochondrial membrane potential that related to an improved calcium buffering capacity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Neuronal deletion of Ppargc1a aggravated neurodegeneration during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
source: Accordingly, neuronal deletion of Ppargc1a aggravated neurodegeneration during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, while neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a ameliorated it.
evidence: This is shown by clinical scores and neuronal counts in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a ameliorated neurodegeneration during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
source: Accordingly, neuronal deletion of Ppargc1a aggravated neurodegeneration during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, while neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a ameliorated it.
evidence: This is demonstrated by clinical scores and neuronal survival data in Figure 5C and 5F.

claim: Neuronal loss occurs from disease onset in multiple sclerosis and correlates best with irreversible disability.
source: Neuronal loss occurs already from disease onset and correlates best with irreversible disability in MS patients (Fisher et al., 2008; Fisniku et al., 2008; Tallantyre et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are currently no therapies available to counteract the progression of neurodegeneration in MS patients.
source: Since there are currently no therapies available to counteract the progression of neurodegeneration in MS patients (Dendrou et al., 2015; Feinstein et al., 2015) and repurposing of drugs to directly target neurodegeneration in MS has been disappointing (Chataway et al., 2020), a better understanding of the molecular processes that determine neuronal cell loss in MS is urgently needed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neuronal loss in MS and EAE has been associated with enhanced production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species by immune cells.
source: Neuronal loss in MS and its animal model, experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), has been associated with enhanced production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species by immune cells and with increased iron accumulation in the gray matter (Stephenson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuronal loss in MS and EAE has been associated with increased iron accumulation in the gray matter.
source: Neuronal loss in MS and its animal model, experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), has been associated with enhanced production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species by immune cells and with increased iron accumulation in the gray matter (Stephenson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Enhanced production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and increased iron accumulation can lead to damage of neuronal mitochondria with subsequent metabolic failure.
source: Both processes can lead to damage of neuronal mitochondria with subsequent metabolic failure (Campbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Postmortem studies of MS patients' CNS tissue revealed compromised neuronal ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation.
source: However, postmortem studies of MS patients' CNS tissue revealed a compromised neuronal ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation as decreased mitochondria complex IV activity in demyelinated axons and neurons was detected (Campbell et al., 2011; Mahad et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Decreased mitochondrial complex IV activity was detected in demyelinated axons and neurons in MS patients.
source: However, postmortem studies of MS patients' CNS tissue revealed a compromised neuronal ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation as decreased mitochondria complex IV activity in demyelinated axons and neurons was detected (Campbell et al., 2011; Mahad et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mitochondrial gene expression is suppressed in motor neurons of the spinal cord in EAE mice.
source: Similarly, mitochondrial gene expression is suppressed in motor neurons of the spinal cord in EAE mice (Schattling et al., 2019), further supporting a comprised mitochondrial function during CNS inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Only a confined group of 29 biological process GO terms showed strong de-enrichment during CNS inflammation in motor neurons.
source: While the majority of terms was enriched during inflammation, only a confined group of 29 terms showed strong de-enrichment (Figure 1A, dashed line) and was dominated by terms representing mitochondrial function (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: De-enriched GO terms during CNS inflammation in motor neurons were dominated by terms representing mitochondrial function.
source: While the majority of terms was enriched during inflammation, only a confined group of 29 terms showed strong de-enrichment (Figure 1A, dashed line) and was dominated by terms representing mitochondrial function (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B displaying top 15 de-enriched GO terms.

claim: There was no difference in mitochondria area normalized to neuronal size in motor neurons between EAE mice and healthy control mice.
source: Therefore, we quantified mitochondria content in the soma of motor neurons in EAE mice at the chronic stage in comparison to healthy control mice, but did not detect any difference in mitochondria area normalized to neuronal size (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transmission electron microscopy analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: There was a tendency towards an increase in overall numbers of motor neuronal mitochondria in EAE mice.
source: However, we detected a tendency towards an increase in overall numbers of motor neuronal mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that was based on an increased size of the neuronal cell body during EAE (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The tendency towards increased mitochondrial numbers was based on an increased size of the neuronal cell body during EAE.
source: However, we detected a tendency towards an increase in overall numbers of motor neuronal mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that was based on an increased size of the neuronal cell body during EAE (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: The size of mitochondria did not differ in motor neurons of healthy and EAE mice.
source: By contrast, the size of mitochondria did not differ in motor neurons of healthy and EAE mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by TEM analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A significant decrease in absolute neuronal complex IV activity was detected in the entire gray matter and ventral horn of acute EAE animals.
source: By analyzing COX histochemistry that represents complex IV activity, we detected a significant decrease in absolute neuronal complex IV activity in the entire gray matter and ventral horn of acute EAE animals (day 15 post immunization) and in chronic EAE animals (day 30 post immunization) in comparison to healthy control mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by COX histochemistry in Figure 1F.

claim: A significant decrease in absolute neuronal complex IV activity was detected in the entire gray matter and ventral horn of chronic EAE animals.
source: By analyzing COX histochemistry that represents complex IV activity, we detected a significant decrease in absolute neuronal complex IV activity in the entire gray matter and ventral horn of acute EAE animals (day 15 post immunization) and in chronic EAE animals (day 30 post immunization) in comparison to healthy control mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by COX histochemistry in Figure 1F.

claim: At day 30 post-immunization, the reduced complex IV activity was partly driven by neuronal loss.
source: Normalization to HuC/HuD-positive neurons revealed that the reduced complex IV activity at day 30 was partly driven by neuronal loss, whereas at day 15 the reduced complex IV activity was independent of neuronal numbers (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is shown by normalized COX histochemistry data in Figure 1G.

claim: At day 15 post-immunization, the reduced complex IV activity was independent of neuronal numbers.
source: Normalization to HuC/HuD-positive neurons revealed that the reduced complex IV activity at day 30 was partly driven by neuronal loss, whereas at day 15 the reduced complex IV activity was independent of neuronal numbers (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is shown by normalized COX histochemistry data in Figure 1G.

claim: Many genes that drive the downregulation of the ETC theme are usually induced by the transcriptional coactivator Ppargc1a.
source: Notably, we detected that many of the genes that drive the downregulation of the ETC theme are usually induced by the transcriptional coactivator Ppargc1a (Lucas et al., 2014; Puigserver et al., 1998; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: Motor neuronal Ppargc1a expression was not altered in acute EAE compared to controls.
source: Motor neuronal Ppargc1a expression itself was not altered in our previously published dataset comparing acute EAE to controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq data in Figure 2B.

claim: A significant increase in phosphorylated-serine570 PGC-1α was detected in spinal cords of acute EAE mice in comparison to healthy control mice.
source: After validation of phosphorylation specificity of the pPGC-1αS570 antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we detected a significant increase in phosphorylated-serine570 PGC-1α in spinal cords of acute EAE mice in comparison to healthy control mice (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed an increase of Ppargc1a-dependent transcriptional targets in primary neurons.
source: Additionally, we revealed that Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed an increase of Ppargc1a-dependent transcriptional targets in primary neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F) and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4 (Cox4i1) and citrate synthase (Cs) in CNS tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression resulted in increased mitochondrial content in primary neurons.
source: Accordingly, neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression resulted in increased mitochondrial content in primary neurons (Figure 3B) and CNS tissue (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mtDNA quantification in Figure 3B.

claim: Neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression resulted in increased mitochondrial content in CNS tissue.
source: Accordingly, neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression resulted in increased mitochondrial content in primary neurons (Figure 3B) and CNS tissue (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mtDNA quantification in Figure 3C.

claim: Neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression resulted in elevated complex IV activity in the gray matter and ventral horn of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice.
source: To determine the mitochondrial activity in these mice, we analyzed whether Ppargc1a-mediated Cox4i1 induction resulted in increased complex IV activity. We detected an elevated complex IV activity in the gray matter and ventral horn of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice, which was not due to a higher number of NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by COX histochemistry in Figure 3D.

claim: Primary neurons of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed an elevated oxygen consumption rate.
source: Metabolically, primary neurons of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed an elevated oxygen consumption rate and maximum respiratory capacity (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1), which was independent of neuronal numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Seahorse metabolic assay in Figure 3E.

claim: Primary neurons of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice retained higher TMRE fluorescence intensity than wild-type controls, representing a hyperpolarized mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: In concordance with higher activity of oxidative phosphorylation, primary neurons of Thy1-Ppargc1a mice retained higher tetramethylrhodamin-ethylester (TMRE) fluorescence intensity than wild-type controls, representing a hyperpolarized mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown by TMRE assay in Figure 3F.

claim: Spontaneously active Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons showed significantly faster clearance of intracellular calcium concentrations compared to wild-type control neurons.
source: By analyzing spontaneously active cortical primary neuronal cultures (cPNC) transduced with the virally encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f (Figure 4A), we recorded a significantly faster clearance of intracellular calcium concentrations and decreased amount of mean calcium in spontaneously active Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons in comparison to wild-type control neurons, whereas the amplitude and number of calcium transients did not differ (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Spontaneously active Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons showed decreased amount of mean calcium compared to wild-type control neurons.
source: By analyzing spontaneously active cortical primary neuronal cultures (cPNC) transduced with the virally encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f (Figure 4A), we recorded a significantly faster clearance of intracellular calcium concentrations and decreased amount of mean calcium in spontaneously active Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons in comparison to wild-type control neurons, whereas the amplitude and number of calcium transients did not differ (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The amplitude and number of calcium transients did not differ between Thy1-Ppargc1a and wild-type neurons.
source: By analyzing spontaneously active cortical primary neuronal cultures (cPNC) transduced with the virally encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6f (Figure 4A), we recorded a significantly faster clearance of intracellular calcium concentrations and decreased amount of mean calcium in spontaneously active Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons in comparison to wild-type control neurons, whereas the amplitude and number of calcium transients did not differ (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is shown by calcium imaging data in Figure 4C.

claim: Neuron-specific Ppargc1a knockout mice showed a more severe EAE disease course compared to control mice.
source: Consequently, neuron-specific Ppargc1a knockout mice (Ppargc1aflx/flx × Eno2Cre+) showed a more severe EAE disease course (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1) and by using NeuN-staining an increased neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn in comparison to Ppargc1aflx/flx control EAE mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by clinical scores in Figure 5A.

claim: Neuron-specific Ppargc1a knockout mice showed increased neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn compared to control EAE mice.
source: Consequently, neuron-specific Ppargc1a knockout mice (Ppargc1aflx/flx × Eno2Cre+) showed a more severe EAE disease course (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1) and by using NeuN-staining an increased neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn in comparison to Ppargc1aflx/flx control EAE mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by NeuN staining quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed a significantly better recovery from clinical disability in comparison to wild-type controls during EAE.
source: EAE induction in Thy1-Ppargc1a and wild-type littermate control mice resulted in a comparable maximum score in the acute phase of the disease. However, Thy1-Ppargc1a mice showed a significantly better recovery from clinical disability in comparison to wild-type controls (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by clinical scores in Figure 5C.

claim: Numbers of infiltrating CD3+ T cells, activated IBA1+ microglia, and MAC-3+ macrophages were similar between Thy1-Ppargc1a and wild-type mice during EAE.
source: Notably, this protection is unlikely to be driven by an impaired immune response as numbers of infiltrating CD3+ T cells, activated IBA1+ microglia, and MAC-3+ macrophages were similar to WT mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by histopathological staining quantification in Figure 5D.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a resulted in a rescue of complex IV activity during acute EAE in the entire gray matter and ventral horn.
source: Moreover, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a resulted in a rescue of complex IV activity during acute EAE in the entire gray matter and ventral horn (Figure 5E), leading to a significant reduction of neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn and more intact axons at day 40 post immunization by using NeuN or HuC/HuD as neuronal marker (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by COX histochemistry in Figure 5E.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a led to a significant reduction of neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn at day 40 post immunization.
source: Moreover, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a resulted in a rescue of complex IV activity during acute EAE in the entire gray matter and ventral horn (Figure 5E), leading to a significant reduction of neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn and more intact axons at day 40 post immunization by using NeuN or HuC/HuD as neuronal marker (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown by neuronal counts in Figure 5F.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a led to more intact axons at day 40 post immunization.
source: Moreover, neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a resulted in a rescue of complex IV activity during acute EAE in the entire gray matter and ventral horn (Figure 5E), leading to a significant reduction of neuronal loss in the gray matter and ventral horn and more intact axons at day 40 post immunization by using NeuN or HuC/HuD as neuronal marker (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown by neurofilament staining in Figure 5F.

claim: PGC-1α can be post-translationally inactivated by phosphorylation at serine 570.
source: Besides quantity, PGC-1α can be post-translationally inactivated by phosphorylation at serine 570 (Li et al., 2007; Xiong et al., 2010), thereby preventing the recruitment of PGC-1α to its regulated promoters, which we tested next.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of PGC-1α at serine 570 prevents the recruitment of PGC-1α to its regulated promoters.
source: Besides quantity, PGC-1α can be post-translationally inactivated by phosphorylation at serine 570 (Li et al., 2007; Xiong et al., 2010), thereby preventing the recruitment of PGC-1α to its regulated promoters, which we tested next.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of PGC-1α at serine 570 could be mediated by increased AKT activity.
source: Increased phosphorylation of serine 570 leads to an inactivation of PGC-1α, which could be mediated by increased AKT activity (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A marked decrease in cortical PGC-1α expression has been reported in MS patients.
source: However, in contrast to MS patients, in which a marked decrease in cortical PGC-1α expression has been reported (Witte et al., 2013), we could not detect a regulation of Ppargc1a in inflamed mouse motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Global Ppargc1a knockout mice showed neurological symptoms such as myoclonus, dystonia, and limb clasping attributed to axonal striatal degeneration.
source: This is in accordance with the global Ppargc1a knockout mice that showed neurological symptoms such as myoclonus, dystonia, and limb clasping that was attributed to axonal striatal degeneration (Lin et al., 2004), although we were not able to detect this phenotype in our neuron-specific Ppargc1a knockout mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ppargc1a overexpression under the Eno2 promoter led to an ameliorated EAE disease course in a recent report.
source: While a recent report using Ppargc1a overexpression under the Eno2 promoter led to an ameliorated EAE disease course (Dang et al., 2019), we believe that this is mainly driven by suppressing the immune response and not by a neuron-intrinsic effect.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Downstream targets of Ppargc1a are repressed in dopaminergic neurons of Parkinson's disease patients.
source: Similarly, downstream targets of Ppargc1a are repressed in dopaminergic neurons of Parkinson's disease patients (Zheng et al., 2010) in which neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a protects dopaminergic neurons in its mouse model (Mudò et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a protects dopaminergic neurons in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
source: Similarly, downstream targets of Ppargc1a are repressed in dopaminergic neurons of Parkinson's disease patients (Zheng et al., 2010) in which neuronal overexpression of Ppargc1a protects dopaminergic neurons in its mouse model (Mudò et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Exercise ameliorates the EAE disease course.
source: Exercise ameliorates the EAE disease course (Klaren et al., 2014; Rossi et al., 2009) and shows several benefits in MS patients (Motl et al., 2017); however, the proof of a neuroprotective effect that is mediated by Ppargc1a induction is currently outstanding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Exercise shows several benefits in MS patients.
source: Exercise ameliorates the EAE disease course (Klaren et al., 2014; Rossi et al., 2009) and shows several benefits in MS patients (Motl et al., 2017); however, the proof of a neuroprotective effect that is mediated by Ppargc1a induction is currently outstanding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mitochondria usually have a high calcium buffering capacity, which is driven by their negative membrane potential generated by oxidative phosphorylation activity.
source: Mitochondria usually have a high calcium buffering capacity, which is driven by their negative membrane potential that is generated by the activity of oxidative phosphorylation (Kann and Kovács, 2007; Zorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Overload of mitochondria with calcium as a consequence of CNS inflammation can result in inappropriate activation of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore with subsequent mitochondrial swelling and cell death.
source: However, overload of mitochondria with calcium as a consequence of CNS inflammation can result in inappropriate activation of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) with subsequent mitochondrial swelling and cell death (Giorgi et al., 2018; Rizzuto et al., 2012), which is one of the neuropathological hallmarks in neurons during EAE (Nikić et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mitochondrial swelling and cell death is one of the neuropathological hallmarks in neurons during EAE.
source: However, overload of mitochondria with calcium as a consequence of CNS inflammation can result in inappropriate activation of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) with subsequent mitochondrial swelling and cell death (Giorgi et al., 2018; Rizzuto et al., 2012), which is one of the neuropathological hallmarks in neurons during EAE (Nikić et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Inhibiting cyclophilin D can partially counteract dysregulation of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.
source: Inhibiting the mitochondrial matrix protein cyclophilin D, a regulator of the PTP can partially counteract this dysregulation (Forte et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuronal mitochondrial deficiency is associated with Alzheimer's disease.
source: As neuronal mitochondrial deficiency is also associated with other neurodegenerative diseases, for example, Alzheimer's disease (Pannaccione et al., 2020), induction of mitochondrial activity could serve as a unifying neuroprotective approach (Murphy and Hartley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Induction of mitochondrial activity could serve as a unifying neuroprotective approach for neurodegenerative diseases.
source: As neuronal mitochondrial deficiency is also associated with other neurodegenerative diseases, for example, Alzheimer's disease (Pannaccione et al., 2020), induction of mitochondrial activity could serve as a unifying neuroprotective approach (Murphy and Hartley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and represents a speculative conclusion.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of sirtuin-1 leads to an ameliorated EAE disease course.
source: Another possible drug candidate is sirtuin-1 that activates PGC-1α by deacetylation, and its neuronal overexpression leads to an ameliorated EAE disease course (Nimmagadda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Sirtuin-1 activates PGC-1α by deacetylation.
source: Another possible drug candidate is sirtuin-1 that activates PGC-1α by deacetylation, and its neuronal overexpression leads to an ameliorated EAE disease course (Nimmagadda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ppargc1a can be induced by intrinsic mechanisms such as cold exposure or exercise.
source: Besides extrinsic induction or activation of Ppargc1a, it can also be induced by intrinsic mechanisms such as cold exposure or exercise (Lin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ocrelizumab and siponimod have been licensed for the treatment of progressive MS patients.
source: Recently, two drugs, ocrelizumab and siponimod, have been licensed for the treatment of progressive MS patients; however, their mode of action relies on immune regulation (Kappos et al., 2018; Montalban et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mode of action of ocrelizumab and siponimod relies on immune regulation.
source: Recently, two drugs, ocrelizumab and siponimod, have been licensed for the treatment of progressive MS patients; however, their mode of action relies on immune regulation (Kappos et al., 2018; Montalban et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Repurposing of drugs to directly target neurodegeneration in MS has been disappointing.
source: Since there are currently no therapies available to counteract the progression of neurodegeneration in MS patients (Dendrou et al., 2015; Feinstein et al., 2015) and repurposing of drugs to directly target neurodegeneration in MS has been disappointing (Chataway et al., 2020), a better understanding of the molecular processes that determine neuronal cell loss in MS is urgently needed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Disruption of neuronal ion homeostasis consumes high amounts of energy that might further drive neuroaxonal injury.
source: Moreover, disruption of neuronal ion homeostasis (Craner et al., 2004; Friese et al., 2014) and aggregation of neuronal proteins (Schattling et al., 2019) consume high amounts of energy that might further drive neuroaxonal injury.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents an inference.

claim: Aggregation of neuronal proteins consumes high amounts of energy that might further drive neuroaxonal injury.
source: Moreover, disruption of neuronal ion homeostasis (Craner et al., 2004; Friese et al., 2014) and aggregation of neuronal proteins (Schattling et al., 2019) consume high amounts of energy that might further drive neuroaxonal injury.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents an inference.

claim: Excessive activation of calcium-dependent processes and neuronal calcium overload is an important component of neuronal injury.
source: Furthermore, excessive activation of calcium-dependent processes and neuronal calcium overload seems to be another important component of neuronal injury (Friese et al., 2007; Schattling et al., 2012; Witte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mitochondria could serve as an important hub as they are pivotal for both energy production and calcium homeostasis.
source: While identifying druggable targets that specifically induce neuronal resilience has been extremely difficult due to insufficient insights into key modulators, mitochondria could serve as an important hub as they are pivotal for both energy production and calcium homeostasis (Vafai and Mootha, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and represents an inference.

claim: Ppargc1a is highly expressed in tissues with high energy demand such as muscle, liver, and CNS.
source: This seems to be particularly relevant in tissues with a high energy demand, for example, muscle, liver, and CNS in which Ppargc1a is highly expressed.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Astrocytes are mostly relying on glycolysis.
source: While astrocytes are mostly relying on glycolysis, neurons mainly generate their energy by oxidative phosphorylation with low glycolytic capacities (Camandola and Mattson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neurons mainly generate their energy by oxidative phosphorylation with low glycolytic capacities.
source: While astrocytes are mostly relying on glycolysis, neurons mainly generate their energy by oxidative phosphorylation with low glycolytic capacities (Camandola and Mattson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mitochondrial damage and inactivation is particularly deleterious for neuronal metabolism.
source: Therefore, mitochondrial damage and inactivation is particularly deleterious for neuronal metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous statement about neuronal energy metabolism.

claim: Rise in neuronal intracellular calcium is one of the hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Besides MS, rise in neuronal intracellular calcium is one of the hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases (Mattson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Several mechanisms lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE, including upregulation of voltage-gated sodium channels and Na+-Ca2+ antiporters.
source: Several mechanisms are relevant that lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE (Siffrin et al., 2015), among them upregulation of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na+-Ca2+ antiporters (Craner et al., 2004), Ca2+ permeable ion channels (Friese et al., 2007; Schattling et al., 2012), and nanoscale ruptures of the axonal plasma membrane (Witte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several mechanisms lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE, including Ca2+ permeable ion channels.
source: Several mechanisms are relevant that lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE (Siffrin et al., 2015), among them upregulation of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na+-Ca2+ antiporters (Craner et al., 2004), Ca2+ permeable ion channels (Friese et al., 2007; Schattling et al., 2012), and nanoscale ruptures of the axonal plasma membrane (Witte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several mechanisms lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE, including nanoscale ruptures of the axonal plasma membrane.
source: Several mechanisms are relevant that lead to intracellular neuronal Ca2+ accumulation in EAE (Siffrin et al., 2015), among them upregulation of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na+-Ca2+ antiporters (Craner et al., 2004), Ca2+ permeable ion channels (Friese et al., 2007; Schattling et al., 2012), and nanoscale ruptures of the axonal plasma membrane (Witte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Calcium uptake by mitochondria holds promise as a therapeutic strategy for several neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Calcium uptake by mitochondria holds the promise as a therapeutic strategy for several neurodegenerative diseases (Lee et al., 2018; Parone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents speculation about therapeutic potential.

claim: Induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity represents an attractive neuroprotective strategy in CNS inflammation by compensating mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Thus, induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity represents an attractive neuroprotective strategy in CNS inflammation by compensating mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal oxidative phosphorylation is compromised during CNS inflammation.
source: Here, we show that neuronal oxidative phosphorylation is compromised during CNS inflammation, which directly contributes to neuronal vulnerability and can be counteracted by induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Compromised neuronal oxidative phosphorylation directly contributes to neuronal vulnerability during CNS inflammation.
source: Here, we show that neuronal oxidative phosphorylation is compromised during CNS inflammation, which directly contributes to neuronal vulnerability and can be counteracted by induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data, particularly the Ppargc1a knockout experiments.

claim: Compromised neuronal oxidative phosphorylation can be counteracted by induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity.
source: Here, we show that neuronal oxidative phosphorylation is compromised during CNS inflammation, which directly contributes to neuronal vulnerability and can be counteracted by induction of neuronal mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Ppargc1a overexpression experiments showing neuroprotection.

claim: Ppargc1a acts as a master switch of mitochondrial function.
source: This compromised oxidative phosphorylation during CNS inflammation is likely coordinated by inactivation of PGC-1α, a transcriptional coactivator that acts as a master switch of mitochondrial function (Mootha et al., 2003; Puigserver et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ppargc1a could act as a switch that modulates oxidative phosphorylation by regulating respective mitochondrial genes under challenging environmental conditions such as CNS inflammation.
source: Thus, tuning Ppargc1a could act as a switch that modulates oxidative phosphorylation by regulating respective mitochondrial genes under challenging environmental conditions, such as CNS inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Prolonged downregulation of mitochondrial gene transcripts will reduce ATP levels that could limit neuronal integrity during chronic inflammation.
source: As a trade-off, prolonged downregulation of mitochondrial gene transcripts will reduce ATP levels that could limit neuronal integrity during chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and established knowledge.

claim: Upregulation of AKT could function as an immediate strategy of neurons against cell death during inflammation.
source: As TNF-α activates the PI3K/AKT pathway (Gu et al., 2006; Li et al., 2017; Osawa et al., 2001), upregulation of AKT could function as an immediate strategy of neurons against cell death during inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to published literature.

claim: TNF-α activates the PI3K/AKT pathway.
source: As TNF-α activates the PI3K/AKT pathway (Gu et al., 2006; Li et al., 2017; Osawa et al., 2001), upregulation of AKT could function as an immediate strategy of neurons against cell death during inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is known to reduce apoptosis and promote survival and proliferation.
source: AKT is activated by phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is known to reduce apoptosis and promote survival and proliferation (Brunet et al., 1999) and thereby counteracts neuronal cell death (Peltier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway counteracts neuronal cell death.
source: AKT is activated by phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is known to reduce apoptosis and promote survival and proliferation (Brunet et al., 1999) and thereby counteracts neuronal cell death (Peltier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AKT1 and AKT3 are mainly expressed in neurons.
source: Three different isoforms of AKT exist. Whereas AKT1 and AKT3 are mainly expressed in neurons, AKT2 is predominantly expressed in astrocytes (Levenga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AKT2 is predominantly expressed in astrocytes.
source: Three different isoforms of AKT exist. Whereas AKT1 and AKT3 are mainly expressed in neurons, AKT2 is predominantly expressed in astrocytes (Levenga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AKT1 has been implicated in late long-term potentiation.
source: So far, the exact function of AKT in neurons is not clear, but AKT1 has been implicated in late long-term potentiation (Levenga et al., 2017) and AKT3 in neuronal growth (Adams et al., 2016; Rivière et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AKT3 has been implicated in neuronal growth.
source: So far, the exact function of AKT in neurons is not clear, but AKT1 has been implicated in late long-term potentiation (Levenga et al., 2017) and AKT3 in neuronal growth (Adams et al., 2016; Rivière et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In Ppargc1a overexpression under the Eno2 promoter, the authors reported a reduced immune cell infiltration, less demyelination, a later EAE onset, and an ameliorated EAE disease course.
source: As Eno2 is also expressed in immune cells and especially T cell function is influenced by altered mitochondrial activity (Buck et al., 2016), in accordance with our notion, the authors reported a reduced immune cell infiltration, less demyelination, a later EAE onset, and an ameliorated EAE disease course (Dang et al., 2019), which are typical features for an immunosuppressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: T cell function is influenced by altered mitochondrial activity.
source: As Eno2 is also expressed in immune cells and especially T cell function is influenced by altered mitochondrial activity (Buck et al., 2016), in accordance with our notion, the authors reported a reduced immune cell infiltration, less demyelination, a later EAE onset, and an ameliorated EAE disease course (Dang et al., 2019), which are typical features for an immunosuppressive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuronal Ppargc1a deletion did not result in different neuronal numbers in healthy mice.
source: Notably, Ppargc1a deletion in neurons did not result in different neuronal numbers in healthy mice by using NeuN staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown by NeuN staining quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression did not influence neuronal numbers in healthy mice.
source: Neuronal Ppargc1a overexpression did also not influence neuronal numbers in healthy mice by using NeuN staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is shown by NeuN staining quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J.

claim: In Thy1-Ppargc1a primary neurons, 11 of the 17 Ppargc1a regulated ETC genes which were downregulated in EAE were induced.
source: Besides Cox4i1, in primary hippocampal neurons, Ppargc1a overexpression induced 11 of the 17 Ppargc1a regulated ETC genes, which were downregulated in EAE (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: The improved calcium buffering capacity in Thy1-Ppargc1a neurons could efficiently rescue calcium overload and neuronal demise.
source: Therefore, the improved calcium buffering capacity in Thy1-Ppargc1a neurons could efficiently rescue calcium overload and neuronal demise, which was indicated by an increased neuronal survival during EAE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging and EAE survival data.

claim: Increased neuronal survival during EAE in Thy1-Ppargc1a mice was indicated by the experimental results.
source: Therefore, the improved calcium buffering capacity in Thy1-Ppargc1a neurons could efficiently rescue calcium overload and neuronal demise, which was indicated by an increased neuronal survival during EAE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuronal counts in Figure 5F.

claim: Pharmacological increase of neuronal mitochondria and oxidative phosphorylation could be a promising neuroprotective strategy.
source: As we detected a higher neuronal resilience in Thy1-Ppargc1a mice during CNS inflammation, pharmacological increase of neuronal mitochondria and oxidative phosphorylation could be a promising neuroprotective strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Some drugs have been described to induce Ppargc1a in different tissues.
source: Some drugs have already been described to induce Ppargc1a in different tissues (Dumont et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2014; Noe et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2012); however, we could not confirm neuronal induction of Ppargc1a by treating mice with bezafibrate or using transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily V member 4 (Trpv4) knockout mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The authors could not confirm neuronal induction of Ppargc1a by treating mice with bezafibrate or using Trpv4 knockout mice.
source: Some drugs have already been described to induce Ppargc1a in different tissues (Dumont et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2014; Noe et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2012); however, we could not confirm neuronal induction of Ppargc1a by treating mice with bezafibrate or using transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily V member 4 (Trpv4) knockout mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data.

claim: Clinical scores correlate better with cervical than lumbar spinal cord lesions in EAE.
source: Cervical spinal cord was used as it was shown that clinical scores correlate better with cervical than lumbar spinal cord lesions in EAE (Fournier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.
